newsitem.title: GERMANY: German assets seen losing allure as tax talks fail.
newsitem.headline: German assets seen losing allure as tax talks fail.

text.p: International investors will be more doubtful about German assets after talks aimed at reforming the country's convoluted tax system collapsed on Wednesday.

Economists said the failure of negotiations between the coalition government and opposition Social Democrats (SPD) will add to financial market concerns that Chancellor Helmut Kohl and his finance minister Theo Waigel face a fierce fight to make Germany's tax and pensions system more flexible.

The direct effect on the mark and on German debt prices will be very limited in the short term, but analysts said uncertainty surrounding the tax regime, coupled with worries about the government's ability to reduce the budget deficit to meet the entry criteria for monetary union (EMU), will hurt sentiment.
"This will make things very difficult for the government if they want to push through austerity measures this year," said Adrian Schmidt, international economist at Chase in London.

With the government failing on Wednesday to force agreement on its proposals, which aim for 30 billion marks ($18 billion) in tax cuts for 1998 and 1999 as well as reform of the pension system, the bill will now probably have to wait until September, when a mediation committee will attempt to hammer out a compromise.

"There was already quite a lot of talk in the market that Germany is really having a terrible time taking some of the more difficult steps towards reforming and making sustainable the social market economic system," said Klaus Baader, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
"So from that perspective, this is certainly not going to do German assets any favours."

While the tax reform bill was aimed at tax cuts next year and beyond, economists said international investment in Germany was likely to be hampered by the lack of clarity now, and that could hurt economic growth this year.
"It will not be much, but it could take 0.1 percent off GDP (in 1997)," said Holger Schmieding, economist at Merrill Lynch in Frankfurt.
Tough words were ringing through the air from both sides on Wednesday, and analysts said the next few months will do little to boost confidence towards Germany or its markets.

Oskar Lafontaine, Germany's opposition leader and seen as the hard man against tax reform, took up the battle cry immdediately after the breakdown of the talk, vowing to fight on and calling the government's bill a "reform against the people and against the economy".
Waigel, for his part, said the government was "absolutely determined to push ahead with its policies".

Economists said this fighting talk was likely to continue for some time, damaging the government's chances of a smooth passage for any additional budget-cutting measures they might feel the need to introduce for this year.

Government forecasts are for a 1997 budget deficit to GDP ratio of 2.9 percent -- just below the 3.0 percent ceiling laid down by the Maastricht Treaty -- but many independent analysts say cripplingly high unemployment and a struugling economic recovery will push the deficit beyond the Maastricht line.

To be sure of meeting the criteria, they say Germany may have to introduce additional spending cuts later this year -- a task which will prove very tough for the government if its relations with the SDP do not improve.
But by the autumn, one or both sides in the tax bill battle will have to back down.
"We may now see some interesting debate within the SDP between Lafontaine, taking a hard line, and Gerhard Schroeder, taking a more moderate line," said Merrill's Schmeiding.
"I think that in fact the main reason the talks failed today is this power struggle within the SPD."

Schmieding said he expected Schroeder, a senior SPD member who had urged his party at the weekend to seek a compromise at Wednesday's talks, to push his line harder in the next few months, forcing the social democrats to soften their stance before the autumn mediation begins. ($ = 1.713 German Marks)
